name: Tabs
description: Switches between views of the same record without leaving the page. The panel below changes; the row above is a widget, not a menu, and the keyboard has to know the difference.
when_to_use: Two to seven sibling views of one thing — an order and its lines, receipts and history. If the views are unrelated, use the sidebar instead. If each view is its own URL, this is navigation and belongs in the django variant.
rules: role="tab" only when the panel is in this document. If each tab is a URL, it is a nav of links with aria-current="page", and nothing else. Putting role="tab" on a link promises a screen reader that arrows will switch panels and Tab will jump into one, and then neither happens.

A tab carries aria-selected, not aria-current. They look interchangeable and are not: aria-current marks where you are in a set of destinations, aria-selected marks which of several panels is showing.

Exactly one tab in the tab order — the selected one gets tabindex 0, the rest get -1. Without this roving tabindex, Tab walks every tab in the row and the panel is seven presses away, which is the opposite of what the pattern exists to do.
Bind the arrow keys. A tablist without them is a row of buttons that only works with a mouse, whatever the roles say.

Activate automatically only when the panels are already in the page. A tab that fetches uses manual activation, or arrowing from the first tab to the seventh fires seven requests and the user reads whichever one lands last.

Manual activation is not only for tabs that fetch. Any tab whose selection has a consequence somebody has to answer — an unsaved form, a confirmation, a job that starts — moves focus on the arrows and commits on Enter or Space. With automatic activation, walking the row raises a dialog the user never asked for, once per tab crossed.

A button that shares the row with the tabs sits outside role="tablist". Everything inside the list is counted as a member of it, so a print button becomes "tab 4 of 4" to a screen reader, and the roving tabindex takes it out of the tab order on top of that.
Generate the ids with $id(). Static ids look fine until a second copy of the same tab set lands on one page, and then two tabs point aria-controls at one panel and nothing reports an error.

htmx attributes cannot be generated by Alpine. htmx processes an element when it first sees it, and a tab rendered by x-for is not in the document then, so its hx-get is inert and the click does nothing at all. A tab that fetches is written out in the markup — which is also why those variants read the row out of the DOM rather than off an array.
Never wrap the row onto a second line. It scrolls sideways, with the next tab peeking, because a second line of tabs reads as a different control.

Below sm, where the labels genuinely do not fit, a native select is the honest control and a scroller is not. A strip is right for six short nouns; for nine phrases it shows two and gives no sign that there are seven more.
Do not colour the inactive tabs. They are text-zinc-600 and nothing else; the active one is the only one carrying weight.
Counts go in a pill on the tab, not in the label, and the pill is tabular-nums so the row does not jitter when a number changes.

A panel that is its own scroller loses its scroll offset the moment x-show hides it: display:none destroys the scroll position rather than remembering it. Read scrollTop before the switch and write it back after, one offset per tab.
x-cloak on every panel that is not the one showing at first paint, or all of them are visible for the moment before Alpine boots.

anatomy.description: The row itself, holding the arrow-key bindings and a label that says what the set is for.
A button when the panel is in this document, a link when the tab is a URL. The two are not interchangeable.
A 2px zinc-900 underline plus the weight change, and nothing else. Inactive tabs are text-zinc-600.
A tabular-nums pill for a number, a 6px dot for a state. Colour on the dot only, per the status rule, and a word beside it in sr-only text.
The region below, tied to its tab by id in both directions, and focusable so it can be reached when it holds no controls.
A button sharing the row with the tabs — print, export, add — and sitting outside the tablist, because the tablist counts its children as tabs.
The question raised when the panel being left holds unsaved input. Its existence is what makes that tab set activate manually.
The scrolling strip a long row becomes on a narrow screen, with the active tab scrolled into view rather than left off the edge — or, past a certain label length, a select instead of a strip.

behaviour: Only the active tab carries weight and colour. Tinting the inactive ones destroys the one distinction the control exists to make.
Two to seven tabs. Past that the row stops being scannable, and views that numerous are usually unrelated, which makes them sidebar entries.

Left and right arrows move between tabs, Home and End jump to the ends, and Tab leaves the row entirely and lands in the panel. That last one is the whole point of the pattern: seven tabs cost one Tab press, not seven.

Activation is automatic when the panels are local, so an arrow both moves and switches. When a tab fetches its panel or has a question to ask first, the arrow moves focus only and Enter or Space commits, which a native button already does.
The row scrolls rather than wraps, and moving by keyboard brings the tab into view. A focused tab off the edge of the strip is a focus ring nobody can see.
Switching does not reload, so the page keeps the scroll position it had. A panel that scrolls inside itself does not keep its own, and has to be handed its offset back after the switch.
Where the tab is part of the record's address it goes in the query string with replaceState, not pushState, so Back leaves the record instead of undoing a tab.
accessibility: role="tablist" on the row, role="tab" on each control, role="tabpanel" on each region, and an aria-label on the tablist naming the set.
Each tab carries aria-selected and aria-controls; each panel carries aria-labelledby pointing back. Both directions, or the panel is announced without its name.
Roving tabindex: the selected tab is 0, every other tab is -1, so Tab enters the row once and leaves into the panel.
Arrow keys move, Home and End jump, and every one of them calls preventDefault so the page does not scroll underneath.
The panel takes tabindex="0" so it is reachable when it contains nothing focusable, which is most panels made of text.

A count or a state mark belongs inside the tab button, where it joins the accessible name — "Receipts 3, 2 lines short". A coloured dot with no words beside it says nothing to a screen reader, and nothing to a person who cannot separate red from grey.
The reason a tab is unavailable is text under the row, tied to the tab with aria-describedby. A title attribute is not an explanation: there is nothing to hover on a phone, and nothing announces it.
aria-labelledby resolves through an element that is display:none, so a panel can keep pointing at the tab that names it even at a width where the tab row is not drawn at all.

Ids come from $id(), so two tab sets on one page cannot cross-wire their aria-controls. Where the ids have to be static — anywhere htmx reads them — they carry a prefix of their own, because two copies of one variant on a page is how a label ends up bound to the wrong control.
